audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Friday, July tenth, twenty twenty-six. Here's what matters today, and the dominant thread is the growing distance between what AI can do and what most people actually experience — which is precisely the gap your practice exists to close.

Let's start there, because Axios published a piece this morning that reads almost like a manifesto for the work you're building. They call it the new AI class divide, and they split the population into three groups: the haves, the have-nots, and — this is the sharp phrase — the know-nots. For frontier power users, AI feels like a revolution. It conjures companies, builds software, solves complex problems at what they describe as warp speed. But for the average person, it's an evolution at best: a smarter search bar, a faster inbox, an ambient layer that saves a few minutes but doesn't fundamentally change anything. And here's the number that should stop you — trillions of dollars in economic value, and the livelihoods of millions of workers, are being staked on a technology that most people neither trust nor fully understand.

Now, why does this matter to you specifically? Because your clients — the enrollment offices, the brokerages, the marketing teams — almost all live on the wrong side of that divide. They are the know-nots, not because they're incapable, but because nobody has translated the frontier into their workflow. That's the entire premise of a consulting practice. And I'd argue this is your lead thought-leadership post of the week. The take isn't "AI is a big deal" — everyone's said that. The take is that the gap between the top few percent of adopters and everyone else is compounding, week over week, and that the organizations stuck at "smarter inbox" are quietly falling behind organizations that have restructured around AI. You could frame it as a diagnostic: which side of the divide is your marketing team on, and what does crossing over actually require? That's a post that positions you as the person who moves people from know-not to have.

Related, and this one is quieter but arguably more important for your governance lane — MIT Technology Review reported that Anthropic has developed a technique they call the Jacobian lens, which gives them the clearest glimpse yet at what's actually happening inside a large language model as it reasons through a problem. What they found ranges, in their words, from the mundane to the unnerving. They discovered a kind of hidden space where the model appears to puzzle over concepts before producing an answer. Now, interpretability research is technical, and it's easy to file under "lab curiosity," but I want you to see the governance angle here. For your FIPPA-bound, public-institution clients, the standard objection to AI adoption has always been "we can't explain how it reaches its conclusions." That objection is now being taken seriously by the labs themselves. The story here isn't that we've solved explainability — we haven't — it's that interpretability is becoming a genuine requirement, not an afterthought. If you're advising a Canadian university or a public body, "we can't fully explain the model" has shifted from a shrug to a documented governance risk. That's a defensible, specific post in your public-institution AI governance lane, and almost none of your competitors are close enough to the research to write it credibly.

And one more in this cluster, because it rounds out the governance picture. Axios also reported that the AI boom is putting Big Tech's transparency to the test — new environmental disclosures from Google, Amazon, and Microsoft show emissions and water use rising as AI infrastructure expands, and, tellingly, the three companies diverge sharply on what they're willing to disclose. I flag this less for a post and more for your situational awareness. When you advise a public institution on procuring AI tools, sustainability disclosure is quietly becoming part of the vendor due-diligence checklist, especially for institutions with their own climate commitments. It's one more line item in the governance conversation, and it's better to see it coming than to be surprised by a procurement officer asking about it.

Moving to higher education, where the international enrolment picture keeps sharpening. ICEF Monitor covered the Institute of International Education's Spring Snapshot, and the headline is that declining demand from India is a major factor behind a softer outlook for foreign enrolment in US higher education for the twenty twenty-six, twenty twenty-seven year. This is the piece I'd sit with. India has been the swing market — the single largest source of the growth that fuelled North American international education for a decade. When Indian demand softens in the US, two things can happen: some of that demand evaporates entirely, and some of it redistributes to competitor destinations. Canada is both a beneficiary and a victim of that dynamic, depending on our own policy posture, which — as we've discussed this week — has been tightening. The strategic question for any Canadian institution is whether they're modelling their pipeline against Indian demand shifts specifically, or just watching aggregate numbers. Most are watching aggregates. The ones that segment by source market see the turn first.

Which connects neatly to a thoughtful piece in The PIE News arguing that recruitment agents are an institution's earliest warning system for changes in student recruitment. The premise is simple but underappreciated: before a demand shift shows up in an enrolment report — which is inherently a lagging indicator, months behind reality — agents on the ground have already seen it, adjusted their advising, and redirected students. The author's argument is that institutions should treat agent intelligence as a leading indicator and build feedback loops to capture it. For your enrollment clients, there's a real operational insight here, and honestly a data-and-AI angle if you want it: the agent network is generating early-warning signal constantly, and most institutions have no structured way to aggregate, analyze, or act on it. That's a gap between raw signal and decision-making — which is exactly the kind of gap AI-assisted analysis is built to close.

And for the competitive backdrop, ICEF also reported that Australia has set its twenty twenty-seven National Planning Level — its cap system — at two hundred ninety-five thousand new international student spaces, even as visa applications from foreign students are falling. I mention it because Australia, Canada, the UK, and the US are all now running some form of managed-growth or cap regime simultaneously. For the first time in a while, every major English-speaking destination is constraining supply at once. That changes the competitive math. When everyone caps, brand and yield efficiency matter more than raw volume — which, again, is your lane. Institutions can no longer grow their way out of a weak brand; they have to convert better within a fixed ceiling.

On to real estate and the macro picture. HousingWire published its RealTrends Verified City Rankings, and the scale is worth noting: nearly seventy-five thousand entries across more than five thousand cities, totalling one-point-six-three trillion dollars in volume and two and a half million transaction sides. Beyond the sheer size, the useful signal is where top agents and teams are concentrating to build scale. For a brokerage, this kind of benchmarking data answers a strategic question — is scale being built in the markets we operate in, or is it migrating elsewhere? It's the sort of dataset that rewards a close read rather than a headline skim.

And the Canadian macro number to watch this morning: Statistics Canada releases June employment data, with economists polled by Reuters expecting a modest gain of around ten thousand jobs after a surprise beat in May. This feeds directly into Bank of Canada rate expectations, and by extension mortgage sentiment. Two consecutive strong prints would complicate the case for further cuts; a weak number reopens it. For your husband's brokerage in Edmonton and Vancouver, and for anyone tracking the commercial investment side, this is the kind of data point that moves financing conditions at the margin. Keep half an eye on it as the morning unfolds.

A couple of marketing notes worth your attention. Adweek ran a piece pushing back on the tired myth that Gen Z has a short attention span. The argument — and I think it's right — is that Gen Z isn't incapable of focus; they're decisive about what earns it. In an over-saturated media environment, they allocate attention deliberately rather than scattering it. The five keys Adweek lays out are practical, but the reframe is the valuable part: stop designing for assumed distraction and start designing for earned attention. That's a useful lens for any brand strategy conversation, including higher-ed brand work, where the audience skews exactly this age.

And from Cannes, Virgin Voyages' marketing lead Nathan Rosenberg made the case that the experience is the brand — that the real marketing isn't the campaign that precedes the experience, it's what happens during and, crucially, after it. It's not a new idea, but it's a well-articulated one, and it's a helpful counterweight in a moment where everyone's obsessing over top-of-funnel AI-generated content. The reminder that the durable brand equity lives in the actual delivered experience is worth carrying into client conversations.

Closer to home in Kamloops, a serious local development: the two people already facing charges in an alleged Kamloops murder plot are now also accused of manufacturing illegal firearms. It's an escalation of a case that's been moving through the local courts, and it's the kind of story worth being aware of simply as a resident of the region. On a more constructive note, a Kamloops visit is helping shape the design of an online support hub for Indigenous entrepreneurs — a small but genuine economic-development signal for the region, and the kind of initiative that occasionally opens doors for local advisory and marketing work.

On the world stage, two things you should have in view. First, a devastating wildfire in southern Spain has killed at least eleven people overnight amid soaring temperatures, with nineteen more unaccounted for, making it one of the deadliest on record there. It's a stark preview of the kind of fire behaviour a hotter climate produces — and a reminder, as we head into our own peak season, of how fast these events turn fatal. Second, an update on the story we covered earlier this week: the US-Iran ceasefire that Trump declared "over" has now given way to intensifying exchanges of fire across the Middle East, raising the risk of a wider conflict and keeping energy markets jittery. For your purposes, the practical read is on oil prices and inflation expectations — a sustained escalation feeds straight into the rate picture we just talked about on the Canadian side.

And finally, one for family safety and local awareness. A wildfire is burning near Boston Bar, in the Fraser Canyon, with local businesses opening early to feed the crews battling it. Boston Bar sits on a corridor plenty of people travel between the Lower Mainland and the interior, so it's worth factoring into any travel plans, and it's a signal that BC's interior fire season is now genuinely active. Given your properties and family across the province, this is the kind of item I'll keep surfacing as conditions develop — early awareness is the whole point.

That's your Friday briefing, Midya. If you do one thing with today's news, sit with the AI class-divide framing — it's the cleanest articulation yet of the problem your practice solves, and it's begging for a post that positions you as the translator between the frontier and the everyday. The higher-ed enrolment signals are quietly telling you that brand and yield efficiency are about to matter more than volume across every major destination at once, which plays to your strengths. And keep the Boston Bar fire on your radar this weekend. I'll be back Monday.
